query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The dominant mechanism governing wear performance in high-entropy-alloy protective coatings is the in situ formation of a stable, protective oxide (or spinel) tribofilm during sliding. This tribofilm acts as a barrier that minimizes direct metal-to-metal contact, thereby lowering wear rates and friction coefficients.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy-alloy coating (e.g., AlCoCrFeNiTi-based or similar composition) without any preformed surface film.
generation.intervention: Conduct controlled sliding (tribological) tests while varying the oxygen partial pressure in the testing environment.
generation.conditions: Tests performed at a constant load, sliding speed, and temperature (with special focus on elevated temperatures above approximately 500 °C up to ~900 °C, where oxidation kinetics are significant), comparing environments with high oxygen partial pressure versus near-inert atmospheres.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, robust oxide or spinel tribofilm on the coating surface during sliding.
generation.mechanism: Increased oxygen partial pressure promotes rapid formation and stabilization of a protective tribofilm. This film reduces direct asperity contact and prevents severe abrasive and adhesive wear by acting as a durable barrier during mechanical contact.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under high oxygen partial pressure (especially at elevated temperatures), the coating will form a well-developed tribofilm that leads to measurable reductions in the wear rate and friction coefficient compared to tests under inert or low oxygen conditions.
generation.baseline: Wear performance (wear rate and friction coefficients) measured in an inert atmosphere (e.g., nitrogen or argon) where oxygen is insufficient to initiate protective tribofilm formation.
generation.boundary: The hypothesized effect should hold over a temperature range from moderate (around 500 °C) to high temperatures (up to approximately 900 °C), as oxidation kinetics become more pronounced; variations in alloy composition or microstructure might shift or limit this range.
generation.uncertainty: It remains uncertain how variations in alloy composition, microstructure, or other processing conditions may affect the specific nature and protective quality of the formed tribofilm. Additionally, in some cases the oxidation may lead to non-protective scales if the oxide phases are not sufficiently coherent or continuous.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a series of sliding wear tests on identical high-entropy-alloy coatings under two controlled environments: one with elevated oxygen partial pressure and one with a near-inert gas atmosphere. Monitor the surface in situ (using high-temperature microscopy or Raman spectroscopy) to track the formation and evolution of any tribofilm. Wear rates and friction coefficients should be measured throughout testing.
measurements: Wear rate (material loss per unit distance or time)
In situ imaging or spectroscopy data to confirm the presence, thickness, and continuity of the tribofilm
Temperature control and oxygen partial pressure readings
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If increasing the oxygen partial pressure does not result in the formation of a continuous, protective tribofilm, or if the wear rate and friction coefficient do not significantly improve compared to the inert baseline (or if they deteriorate), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. High-entropy alloys (HEAs), since their discovery by Yeh et al. in 2004, [1] have opened up researchers to a new alloy system that contains five or more equimolar principal elements. In equimolar HEAs, each element has an equal probability of occupying the lattice sites in a crystal structure such as face-centered cubic (FCC), [2] body-centered cubic (BCC), [3] or hexagonal structure [4] crystal structures. Lattice distortion, sluggish diffusion, high entropy, and cocktail effects have been identified as the core effects contributing to the superior properties, hardness, strength, ductility, erosion, tribocorrosion, corrosion, and oxidation/wear resistance [5] − [7] of HEAs in a wide range of temperatures over conventional alloys. From the viewpoint of applications in extrusion dies and cutting inserts, the cost of metal powders used to develop bulk HEAs can hinder their commercialization as an alternative to the alloys in use. Abstract High entropy or compositionally complex alloys provide opportunities for optimization towards new high-temperature materials. Improvements in the equiatomic alloy Al 17 Co 17 Cr 17 Cu 17 Fe 17 Ni 17 (at.%) led to the base alloy for this work with the chemical composition Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 (at.%). Characterization of the beneficial particle-strengthened microstructure by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and observation of good mechanical properties at elevated temperatures arose the need of accomplishing further optimization steps. For this purpose, the refractory metals hafnium and molybdenum were added in small amounts (0.5 and 1.0 at.% respectively) because of their well-known positive effects on mechanical properties of Ni-based superalloys. By correlation of microstructural examinations using SEM with tensile tests in the temperature range of room temperature up to 900 °C, conclusions could be drawn for further optimization steps. Keywords: HEA, high entropy alloys, compositionally complex alloys, mechanical characterization

decision.trend: Early work (2019) on AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 high-entropy alloy coatings (PMC7515071) demonstrated that wear resistance improves at high temperatures because a protective spinel tribofilm forms on the surface. Subsequent studies (2020, PMC7304825) used nanocrystalline CuMoTaWV refractory high-entropy alloy films, confirming that controlling surface structure and hardness can enhance tribological performance. Efforts have progressively moved from powder-based approaches to magnetron sputtering, focusing on how oxide or spinel films form under sliding contact. Although these results highlight that tribofilms significantly affect wear, the exact mechanism governing their formation, stability, and protective function remains partially unresolved, particularly under elevated temperatures and variable environments.
decision.unsolved: It is still unclear how the dynamic formation and stability of oxide- or spinel-based tribofilms primarily control wear performance of high-entropy-alloy coatings across different temperature and load regimes. A single testable mechanistic hypothesis is that the key factor governing wear performance is the in situ formation of a stable, protective oxide or spinel tribofilm at the contact surface, which reduces direct metal-to-metal contact and prevents severe abrasive and adhesive wear. A controlled change distinguishing this hypothesis from a baseline would be to vary the oxygen partial pressure during sliding while keeping composition, load, and speed constant. If the hypothesis is correct, coatings tested at higher partial oxygen pressures (where robust oxide/spinel tribofilms should form) will exhibit measurably lower wear rates and friction coefficients than the same coatings in near-inert atmospheres. This effect should be most pronounced at elevated temperatures (above ~500 °C), where oxidation kinetics increase. Previous studies (PMC7515071, PMC7304825) show that oxide-spinel tribofilms are protective, supporting this hypothesis. A decisive falsification would occur if no improvement in wear resistance or friction is observed when oxygen partial pressure is increased, or if a protective tribofilm does not form under conditions favorable to oxide formation.
decision.lever: Conduct real-time tribological tests under precisely controlled partial oxygen pressures and temperatures (room temperature to ~900 °C) using in situ surface imaging (e.g., high-temperature microscopy or Raman spectroscopy) to directly observe formation and evolution of the tribofilm during sliding.
decision.why: This approach directly addresses the hypothesized controlling effect of protective tribofilm on wear performance. By systematically modulating oxygen availability and tracking tribofilm nucleation and growth in real time, the influence of tribofilms can be isolated. A strong correlation between tribofilm formation at higher oxygen levels (and temperatures) and reduced wear would validate the hypothesis and guide further optimization of high-entropy-alloy protective coatings for demanding applications.
